transcript:
Header: 2025-06-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Sam Ortega (Glacier Lead ML Eng), Marta Liu (CTO), Kevin Park (Infra)
---
Summary: Technical deep dive focused on autoscaling semantics for inference pools: burst policies, queue/backpressure models, reserved GPU sizing, and runtime knobs (batching, KV cache, quantization). Customer requested concrete guidance for a 2-week pilot and SLOs for payments autopay flow (high QPS, strict P95).
Topics: autoscale policies, warm pools, queueing/backpressure, kv cache hit strategies, quantization tradeoffs, private VPC constraints, bench links shared (redwood.com/bench/glacier-spreadsheet).

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intros and then we'll jump into the capacity questions.
[00:18] Marta (Glacier CTO): thanks Alex. we are mainly concerned about a payment flow that needs sub-300ms p95 for inference. that's the hard req, while keeping cost reasonable.
[00:31] Sam (Glacier): and we have spikes during batch payroll windows and month-ends, so burstability is critical, also our infra team prefers VPC-only access.
[00:45] Priya (Redwood SE): yeah, got it. we'll cover both hosted and private deployment tradeoffs; pros/cons for reserved GPUs vs purely burst pools. quick note: recorded benchmark spreadsheet is in the meeting notes link.
[01:02] Kevin (Infra): do you need sys access for the pilot or just API endpoints? we have strict egress rules.
[01:10] Alex: for the first two tests API key + staging VPC peering is fine. later we can do an on-prem agent if needed.

[02:05] Priya: starting with the runtime baseline — at small context lengths (<2k tokens) our A10-class instances get ~50–100 tok/s depending on quant. once you go 8k it drops and KV cache becomes critical to reduce recomputation of prefix states.
[02:22] Sam: can you explain the KV cache a bit more? our current system doesn't expose a split cache.
[02:28] Priya: sure. the KV cache we mean is the key/value attention cache that the model runtime keeps for each active session to avoid recomputing earlier tokens. in Redwood we have automatic per-route prefix caching and global shard-level caches. hit rate is what really moves the needle — with >70% hit you'll see P95 improve a lot.
[02:55] Sam: so cache hit is per-user session? we have short-lived sessions for payment checks.
[03:01] Priya: yes, it's per conversation/session id. for short-lived sessions you can still benefit from prefix caching if you use a shared system prompt or reuse recent prefixes across similar flows. otherwise you'll rely more on batching and lower-latency models.

[04:00] Marta: we saw mention of batching in the doc. we need deterministic latencies—does batching add jitter?
[04:10] Priya: batching introduces a tradeoff. for steady qps batching reduces cost and average latency but can add jitter to p95 if you wait to fill batches. Redwood's runtime uses timeout-based batching with adaptive thresholds: it will flush at e.g., 3ms or when batch size 8 reached. you can configure strict low-latency mode (flush at 0.5ms) but that increases cost.
[04:42] Kevin: what's the real-world p95 impact? numbers please.
[04:48] Priya: example: on an A10 with a quantized Llama2-13B variant, unbatched single request p95 might be ~180ms for short contexts; with adaptive batching tuned for throughput you might see avg latency drop to 110ms but p95 widen to 260–320ms if spikes cause batching to buffer. strict low-latency config keeps p95 ~190–220ms but costs ~1.8x more tokens/hour. these are approximations from our prod benchmarks.

[06:00] Alex: let's talk autoscaling model — Glacier's spike shapes? Kevin?
[06:06] Kevin: typical baseline 300 qps on weekdays, bursts to 8k qps for ~20–60min at month-end. also some microbursts during customer checkout spikes lasting seconds.
[06:20] Priya: okay that matters. Redwood supports a two-tier pool model: reserved pool (warm reserved GPUs) sized for baseline + scheduled autoscale, and burst pool (cold or thin-function) for short peaks. recommended: reserve capacity for ~1.2x baseline to handle steady load and warm short-burst pool for the first N requests while autoscaler spins up more GPUs.
[06:45] Sam: how do you handle cold starts? they kill latency.
[06:48] Priya: we mitigate by keeping a small warm standby of minimal replicas (warm pool). cold start for a new GPU is around 20–90s depending on model and quant strategy; warm pool removes that. for very low-latency service we recommend a reserved fleet with ability to scale horizontally via quick warm replicas + fast model warm caching.

[08:00] Marta: backpressure and queueing — we currently use a leaky-bucket in our API gateway. what would you recommend?
[08:12] Priya: two common approaches: queueing with priority + admission control vs immediate 429-style backpressure. Redwood offers a soft-queue where requests are enqueued with per-route priority and max wait thresholds. policy rules: hard SLO routes (payments) get priority slices in the reserved pool and are allowed a short wait (e.g., 200–400ms) before rerouting to failover model; background routes are queued longer or dropped.
[08:46] Sam: you said reroute to a failover model — how does that work?
[08:50] Priya: we maintain compatible smaller model variants (quantized or distilled) that can serve as fallbacks. the router evaluates capacity and latency budget then automatically selects the fallback if serving on full model would break p95. logs capture the decision and we emit alerts when fallbacks exceed X%.

[10:10] Alex: what about model quantization — effect on perf and quality?
[10:15] Priya: quantization (8-bit or 4-bit) reduces memory by ~2–4x and increases throughput; however some tasks see small quality regressions. we recommend token-level evals on representative prompt sets. for payments we usually try 8-bit first and validate with Redwood Optimize's regression tests. if quality drops we either shrink model size or use mixed-precision where hot layers keep fp16.
[10:45] Marta: any guidance on GPU types and reserved sizing? A10 vs A100?
[10:50] Priya: A10 is good for cost-effective inference at 8–13B models; A100 benefits heavy throughput and large context lengths or 70B+ models. reserved pool suggestion: for your baseline 300 qps, assuming 8k context and conservative batching, start with 4–6 A10s reserved and a burst pool that can scale to 16 A10-equivalent on demand. we'll provide modeling numbers in the spreadsheet.

[12:20] Kevin: can Redwood autoscaler respect our VPC egress and IAM? we can't call out to public endpoints.
[12:27] Priya: yes in Private deployments we can install the control plane in your VPC or run an air-gapped on-prem package. the autoscaler operates on your internal cluster and we provide the same routing policies. there are some feature parity notes (we'll document them).

[13:50] Sam: curious about queueing math — how do you set thresholds so that p95 isn't violated during ramp-ups?
[13:57] Priya: we use a hybrid queue + probabilistic admission model: compute expected service time per request from recent telemetry, then set a max queue wait such that (expected_wait + expected_service) <= p95_budget for that route. example: if p95 budget is 300ms and expected service 180ms, max wait 120ms. requests exceeding wait are either redirected to fallback or return 429. This is a simple M/M/c approximation with real-time corrective factors.

[15:20] Alex: data retention and RBAC — Glacier asked about logs for audit.
[15:25] Marta: SOC2 is a hard requirement.
[15:27] Alex: Redwood supports audit logs, encryption at rest, KMS integrations and SSO/SAML. private deployments can integrate with your HSM. we'll include the security whitepaper.

[16:30] Priya: demo note: we'll run a short perf run on staging using 1k rps with a traffic shape you provide. keep in mind payload sizes change perf — e.g., short 32 token prompts are way easier than 1k token contexts.
[16:45] Sam: our payment flow average prompt ~120 tokens plus 4–8kb of context metadata.
[16:52] Priya: ok that'll be helpful. also send a sample of the real prompts for quality checks.

[18:00] Alex: on pricing — reserved vs pure hosted burst?
[18:05] Priya: reserved pools are committed monthly and cheaper per-hour; burst pools (on-demand) are higher unit cost. hybrid is common: reserve baseline, burst on demand for rare peaks. Redwood also has 'pre-warmed burst' credits which are cheaper than pure on-demand but billed by hour. we'll put example numbers in the pricing deck.

[19:40] Kevin: what about autoscale cooldowns and oscillation? we want to avoid thrashing (spin-ups/downs).
[19:49] Priya: we advise multi-window scaling and ramp-up smoothing: require sustained threshold exceedance across short (30s), medium (3m), and long (10m) windows before scaling heavy. also scale out faster than scale in and keep a minimum graceful drain time for replicas. our default scale-in cooldown is 8–12 minutes.

[21:10] Sam: how does prefix/KV cache eviction work under memory pressure?
[21:16] Priya: eviction is LRU with policy tiers: pinned prefixes (system prompts), session-scoped prefixes, and global learned prefixes. under memory pressure we evict lowest-value prefixes first. you can pin certain conversation contexts if you expect repeats.

[22:40] Marta: what observability will we get to make decisions?
[22:45] Priya: Redwood Console exposes token/time cost breakdown, per-route p50/p95/p99, KV cache hit rate, batch sizes, queue lengths, and model fallback counts. we'll also export raw traces to your OTLP stack if you want.

[24:00] Alex: let's discuss a concrete pilot plan. Priya?
[24:05] Priya: two-week pilot: week 1 baseline perf tests in staging with reserved 4 A10s + 2 warm standby and an on-demand burst pool; sample traffic shape from Kevin. we'll collect p50/p95/p99 latency, KV hit %, batch distribution, fallback rate. week 2 run month-end-scale emulation up to 8k qps for short windows and validate failover and billing.

[25:20] Kevin: how do we safely emulate 8k without harming our infra?
[25:24] Priya: Redwood provides a load generator in your VPC or we can accept anonymized replay traces. we also sandbox the test to our staging cluster or your staging VPC.

[26:40] Sam: are there success metrics you recommend?
[26:45] Priya: yes, define SLOs: p95 <= 300ms for payments with fallback <1% and fallback quality delta <= 1% on the eval set. KV hit rate target >65–75% for pronounced gains. cost per 1M tokens is another metric to track.

[28:00] Marta: any gotchas with quantization and warm pools?
[28:05] Priya: quantized models can increase warm load times slightly due to extra kernel setup, but overall memory smaller so you fit more replicas per GPU. just test end-to-end and use Redwood Optimize to recommend quant profile.

[29:15] Alex: competitor question — do you compare fallback quality with Anthropic or ManagedCloudAI?
[29:22] Priya: we have benchmark comparisons but quality varies by prompt. we include model choice guidance but recommend you do evals with your real prompts.

[30:40] Kevin: what about cost ceilings? can we set hard budget limits that will enforce degradation policies?
[30:46] Priya: yes, Redwood has policy controls: budget caps can automatically reduce model size (downgrade to small model), reject non-essential routes, or restrict batch sizes. those are tunable per-account or per-route.

[32:00] Sam: a little worried about the complexity of tuning all these knobs. can Redwood provide default safe configs?
[32:06] Priya: absolutely. we ship opinionated templates: low-latency, cost-optimized, and balanced. you can start with 'low-latency' for payments and 'cost-optimized' for other paths, then iterate with telemetry.

[33:30] Marta: from a compliance view, we need all logs stored for 12 months. is that possible?
[33:35] Alex: yes enterprise retention is supported; in Private you can control retention and export to S3 or the internal archive.

[34:40] Priya: small note on batch sizing heuristics — runtime maintains per-worker dynamic batch counters and will split large sequences to avoid OOM. also it can do micro-batching for streaming workloads to keep latency low.

[36:00] Kevin: for the pilot, what sample size of prompts do you need for quality eval?
[36:05] Priya: 500–1,000 representative prompts across the flows should be enough for an initial estimate; we'll run automated evals and generate regression alerts.

[37:20] Sam: are there any hard limits on concurrent sessions per GPU?
[37:24] Priya: limits depend on model size and context; for 13B quantized on A10 you might handle hundreds of concurrent short sessions, but with 8k context it's tens. we'll model exact numbers for your payloads.

[38:45] Alex: quick callouts — action items recap in a bit. any other tech questions?
[38:52] Marta: last one: if we need to go full on-prem later, migration complexity?
[38:58] Priya: we designed the API and routing to be identical across Hosted/Dedicated/Private. migration requires plan for data plane (on-prem k8s) sizing and a control-plane handoff; Redwood provides runbooks and on-site assistance.

[40:10] Sam: small transcription-ish question: you said KV cache hit target 65–75% — how achievable is that?
[40:15] Priya: depends on session reuse. with shared system prompts and pinned prefixes typical customer workloads hit 70–80% after tuning. if sessions are one-off it's lower.

[41:30] Alex: ok, let's do a quick timeline — Kevin will share traffic shapes by 2025-06-16, Priya runs baseline stress by 6/18, Alex shares pricing by 6/20, pilot start 6/23.
[41:45] Kevin: agreed.

[43:00] Marta: one last thing — we want the decision matrix to be explicit: when to choose reserved vs burst only.
[43:06] Priya: we'll include a decision table in the follow-up: considerations (SLO strictness, burst frequency/duration, cost constraints, compliance) and recommended architecture.

[44:30] Sam: can you capture where fallback quality might affect transaction failure rates? that's a business metric for us.
[44:36] Priya: yes we'll run the eval and produce expected error deltas. also set a monitoring alert for fallback-induced error increase >0.5%.

[46:00] Alex: closing — any blockers?
[46:05] Kevin: only that we need the staging VPC peering info.
[46:08] Alex: we'll follow up in email for peering.

[47:30] Priya: quick note: I'll attach a runbook for queueing policy examples and a sample nginx ingress config for soft-queue behavior in the staging docs link.

[48:10] Sam: thanks all, useful session. small transcription error: earlier you said 'A one-o' meaning A100?
[48:18] Priya: yes, sorry that was garbled. I meant A100 for heavy throughput and large contexts.

[49:20] Alex: final recap in chat: next steps and owners.
[49:28] Marta: thanks everyone.
[50:00] End of recording.
